text.p: The dollar was bid higher in European trading on Monday after sliding quite sharply in the Far East in the wake of Saturday's Group-of-Seven (G7) meeting, and many financial analysts see its recent firmer trend continuing.
The market had long dollar positions ahead of the meeting and the overnight dip reflected little more than some of those positions being pared back, dealers said.
"It is very well bid this morning," said Nick Parsons, currency strategist at Banque Paribas. "I don't think the market is going to give this up at the first attempt."

The official statement issued by the seven nations said "We discussed the developments on currency and financial markets. We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets, noted in our April 1995 communique, have been corrected."
There was no talk of intervention, concerted or unilateral, and economic fundamentals still argue for a firmer dollar.

"Whatever G7 wish, they can't wish away the interest rate differential, they can't wish away the growth cycles and they can't wish away the generally more favourable attitude for U.S. assets," Paribas' Parsons said.

The dollar dipped to 1.6350 marks and 120.40 yen overnight in the immediate aftermath of the meeting statement but by 1100 GMT it had clawed back almost two pfennigs to 1.6520 and more than two yen to 122.75.

Dollar/mark is seen having more upside potential than dollar/yen given that of the G7 nations, Japan is the most worried about the weakness of its currency versus the dollar and the most likely to intervene.
Japan's external reserves stood at $217 billion in January so it has plenty of ammunition.
"If you play dollar/yen you could well find the BoJ is the counter-party," said one dealer.
An example of the economic imbalance that will tend to keep the dollar firm came this morning with Japan private machinery orders.

Machinery orders fell a seasonally adjusted 12.8 percent in December and the Economic Planning Agency said it expected private machinery orders in the same category to fall 8.5 percent in the January-March quarter.
"This is why the G7 statement was more an expression of hope than of determination," said one analyst. "But the next few days will be nervous as is always the case after a G7 meeting."

"Beyond the initial impact, the G7 is likely to have little more effect than slowing the dollar's rise, as markets become more cautious and perhaps fearful of intervention," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
He noted that there was a chance of a U.S. rate increase soon and even if there were not, there was no prospect of a rise in either Germany or Japan to support their currencies.

Generally, traders were looking for a fairly rapid move back to the 1.6750 mark and 125 yen areas reached last Friday, although above 125 the market will start to become extremely wary of Bank of Japan intervention.
